Reding Quiñones, the US attorney in the Southern District of Florida tapped to oversee a sweeping "grand conspiracy" probe targeting federal officials involved in past Trump investigations, has resigned, Attorney General Todd Blanche announced Friday on X. sources.news_title: Two Senior DOJ Officials Resign, Including U.S. Attorney Overseeing John Brennan Russiagate Investigation
sources.text:
The departures of federal prosecutor Jason Reding Quiñones and National Security Division chief John Eisenberg follow the resignation of Civil Rights Division head Harmeet Dhillon, leaving three senior Justice Department positions vacant within two days.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
WASHINGTON — Two senior Justice Department officials resigned Friday, Nov. 6, including the federal prosecutor overseeing an investigation into former CIA Director John Brennan and other officials involved in past investigations of President Donald Trump, marking the latest departures from the department following Republicans’ sweeping midterm election losses.
Jason Reding Quiñones, U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida, and John Eisenberg, assistant attorney general for the National Security Division, submitted their resignations to Attorney General Todd Blanche. Their departures came one day after Harmeet Dhillon stepped down as head of the department’s Civil Rights Division.
Blanche confirmed Quiñones’ resignation in a public statement but did not provide a reason for his departure.
“United States Attorney for the Southern District of Florida Jason Reding Quiñones submitted his resignation from the Department of Justice,” Blanche announced Friday.
“We are grateful for Jason’s leadership in combatting violent crime, drug trafficking, sex trafficking, and transnational crime, including the indictment of Raúl Castro. Jason has served the Department multiple times over his distinguished career, and we thank him for his service to this country,” he added.
Quiñones had supervised the department’s investigation into whether officials from previous Democratic administrations improperly used federal intelligence and law enforcement agencies to target Trump.
The investigation, internally described as the “grand conspiracy” probe, has examined the origins of the Russia investigation involving Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign, as well as subsequent federal investigations into the president.
A related investigation has focused on whether Brennan provided false testimony to Congress concerning the CIA’s role in preparing a 2017 intelligence assessment of Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election.
According to CBS News’ Nov. 6 reporting, Quiñones’ resignation comes after months of disagreements among prosecutors and senior Justice Department officials over the investigation’s management and the strength of available evidence.
The inquiry has involved grand jury proceedings in Fort Pierce, Florida, but has not produced criminal charges establishing the alleged conspiracy.
Brennan was subpoenaed in September to appear before a federal grand jury, according to earlier CBS News reporting.
His attorneys have challenged the investigation, arguing that it is politically motivated and lacks sufficient evidence to support criminal prosecution.
Quiñones’ departure follows several previous changes involving prosecutors assigned to the investigation.
Former federal prosecutor Joseph diGenova, who had been appointed to oversee the inquiry, resigned in September following disagreements with senior Justice Department leadership.
DiGenova’s departure came amid reported frustration over the investigation’s pace and disagreements concerning the evidence needed to support potential charges.
Kurt Olsen, a former White House attorney involved in the investigation, subsequently left the case, while other temporarily assigned prosecutors returned to their original offices.
Earlier this year, career prosecutor Maria Medetis Long was removed from the Brennan investigation after reportedly expressing concerns about the strength of the evidence.
The repeated personnel changes have raised questions about whether the department can advance the investigation toward potential indictments.
Blanche previously dismissed suggestions that the departures reflected significant internal disagreements, maintaining that the investigation would continue.
Quiñones had also supervised other high-profile federal cases in South Florida, including the indictment of former Cuban leader Raúl Castro and five other individuals in connection with the 1996 downing of two civilian aircraft.
He established a Cuba-focused task force and oversaw investigations involving international organized crime, drug trafficking and corruption.
His resignation leaves the Southern District of Florida without its Senate-confirmed chief federal prosecutor while the department determines how to continue several politically sensitive investigations.
The second resignation Friday involved Eisenberg, who directed the Justice Department’s National Security Division.
Blanche announced that he had accepted Eisenberg’s resignation and praised his work addressing domestic and international security threats.
“Today I accepted the resignation of Assistant Attorney General for the National Security Division John Eisenberg from the Department of Justice. He has served with distinction, strengthening our nation’s ability to address threats, both foreign and domestic,” Blanche said.
“Under his leadership, the Division advanced President Trump’s mission to make America safe by prosecuting terrorists and working with our law enforcement partners to disrupt planned attacks on the American people.”
Blanche also acknowledged Eisenberg’s previous service in the Trump administration.
“This marks John’s second tour of duty serving President Trump as a national security official and advisor. We are grateful for his many years of commitment to protecting our nation and wish him continued success.”
Eisenberg previously served as a senior national security lawyer during Trump’s first presidential term.
His Justice Department division was responsible for major cases involving espionage, terrorism, cybersecurity and the protection of classified information.
The division also handled the prosecution of former national security adviser John Bolton over allegations involving the mishandling of classified material.
According to Reuters’ Nov. 6 report, neither Quiñones nor Eisenberg publicly explained the reasons for resigning.
Their departures follow Thursday’s resignation of Dhillon, who had led the department’s Civil Rights Division and implemented substantial changes to federal civil rights enforcement priorities.
Dhillon’s departure was announced as Democrats prepared to investigate the administration’s handling of civil rights cases, immigration enforcement and federal agency operations.
The three resignations leave vacancies in divisions responsible for national security, civil rights enforcement and major federal criminal investigations.
The timing follows Tuesday’s midterm elections, which gave Democrats control of both chambers of Congress beginning in January 2027.
Incoming Democratic committee leaders have announced plans to investigate the Justice Department’s operations, including allegations that the administration used federal law enforcement authorities against political opponents.
Those investigations could involve requests for internal communications, testimony from senior officials and examinations of prosecutorial decisions.
Republicans have defended the department’s investigations into former intelligence officials, arguing that questions about the origins and handling of the Trump-Russia investigation warrant further examination.
However, the allegations under investigation remain unproven, and no charges have been filed establishing the broader conspiracy described by administration officials.
The resignations also complicate the department’s leadership transition as it prepares for increased congressional oversight.
According to The Associated Press, the departures add to a broader series of personnel changes following the election, although senior officials have not publicly attributed the resignations to the results.
For now, the Brennan investigation remains unresolved, with prosecutors facing questions about the evidence, repeated personnel departures and whether additional grand jury proceedings will take place.
The Justice Department has not announced permanent replacements for Quiñones or Eisenberg.

sources.news_title: Top DOJ National Security Division Lawyer Abruptly Resigns
sources.text:
John Eisenberg, the Justice Department’s assistant attorney general for national security, resigned abruptly Friday, according to the department.
Attorney General Todd Blanche announced Eisenberg’s departure on X and praised him for “strengthening our nation’s ability to address threats, both foreign and domestic.”
Eisenberg became the second assistant attorney general to leave the department this week, just two days after Democrats swept the midterm elections and regained control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate.
On Thursday, Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general overseeing the Civil Rights Division, submitted her resignation. Dhillon had informed the White House before the election that she planned to step down.
Jason Reding Quiñones, a Trump-appointed U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida, also resigned Friday.
Unlike Dhillon, Eisenberg kept a relatively low public profile during his time leading the National Security Division, which has seen a significant exodus of career employees over the past year.
Late last year, the division was placed in the difficult position of overseeing redactions to millions of pages of investigative records involving accused sex trafficker Jeffrey Epstein. Congress ordered the massive review as pressure mounted to release the files.
The effort later expanded to include personnel from other Justice Department components, including the FBI, the Criminal Division and the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Manhattan. Together, those offices assigned 400 attorneys to examine roughly 5.2 million pages.
The redactions have drawn intense criticism. Several of Epstein’s victims said their names and personal information were mistakenly made public, while members of Congress accused the department of improperly concealing details about potential unindicted co-conspirators.
MORE ON THIS: Couple Devastated After Toddler Dies in Apartment Window Fall
Established several years after the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, the National Security Division oversees the Justice Department’s counterterrorism and counterintelligence operations, enforces export controls and reviews foreign investments in U.S. companies.
U.S. attorney’s offices across the country must consult the division—and in some cases obtain its approval—when pursuing certain national security matters.
Since President Trump took office in January, the National Security Division has been involved in several high-profile cases, including leak investigations targeting journalists such as Washington Post reporter Hannah Natanson. Her home was searched earlier this year during an Espionage Act investigation involving a government contractor.
The division has also been central to sweeping changes in domestic terrorism investigations ordered last year by then-Attorney General Pam Bondi.
In December, Bondi directed law enforcement agencies and federal prosecutors to prioritize investigations and prosecutions involving people and groups associated with the anti-fascist antifa movement or labeled “extremist.”
Her directive expanded the range of conduct that could be investigated as domestic terrorism, including doxxing law enforcement officers or participating in a parade intended to obstruct the administration of justice.
This year, the National Security Division helped bring the first-ever case before the Alien Terrorist Removal Court, a secretive federal immigration court created decades ago that relies on classified evidence to deport suspected “alien terrorists,” including people who have never been charged with a crime.
Before the court could consider the constitutional boundaries of the case, however, the target, Nazira Haji Zada, agreed to deportation to Afghanistan rather than challenge the government’s allegation that she was an “alien terrorist.”

WASHINGTON (AP) — The top federal prosecutor in Miami who had been tasked with overseeing an investigation into foes of President Donald Trump has resigned, joining other high-profile Justice Department officials departing in the wake of the midterm elections, officials said Friday.
Jason Reding Quiñones’ resignation follows frustrations among Washington officials with his management of the office assigned to lead the so-called “grand conspiracy” investigation, according to people familiar with the matter who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss personnel issues.
The Justice Department’s top national security official, John Eisenberg, also resigned on Friday, Attorney General Todd Blanche said. On Thursday, Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, who led a radical overhaul of the department’s Civil Rights Division , also announced her departure.
Quiñones was confirmed by the Senate last year as U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida, where the Justice Department had centered its meandering probe into whether former law enforcement and intelligence officials conspired against the Republican president.
His departure comes as the investigation has shown signs of faltering amid a spate of staff turnovers and delays. Investigators in recent weeks have put off scheduled grand jury testimony of several witnesses, according to multiple people familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation.
Blanche said in a social media post that the department is grateful for Quiñones’ “leadership in combating violent crime, drug trafficking, sex trafficking, and transnational crime, including the indictment of Raúl Castro.”
Castro, the former Cuban president, was indicted by Quiñones’ office in May on charges related to the 1996 downing of civilian planes flown by Miami-based exiles.
Quiñones said Friday that he is leaving with “immense pride in what we accomplished together and profound gratitude for the opportunity to serve our great Nation.”
“I am grateful to President Trump for his trust and to the extraordinary men and women of the great Southern District of Florida for their dedication, friendship, and unwavering commitment to justice and the rule of law,” Quiñones wrote in a social media post.
The “grand conspiracy” investigation has proceeded in fits and starts for over a year with repeated setbacks and departures. Last April, a lead national security prosecutor in the investigation of former CIA Director John Brennan was replaced on the team after raising questions about the strength of the case.
Shortly afterward, Joseph diGenova, a former U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, took over the probe. DiGenova resigned from the Justice Department in September without bringing any criminal charges.
Eisenberg was sworn in as assistant attorney general in charge of the department’s National Security Division in June 2025 and oversaw cases involving espionage, terrorism, export control violations, cyber crimes and other matters.
Among the division’s most high-profile cases under his watch was the prosecution of former national security adviser John Bolton, who pleaded guilty this year to allegations of mishandling classified information and is awaiting sentencing.
“He has served with distinction, strengthening our nation’s ability to address threats, both foreign and domestic,” Blanche said in a statement.

sources.text:
Jason Reding Quinones resigns as US Attorney for Southern Florida amid controversy over Trump's election conspiracy probe
Jason Reding Quiñones has stepped down as U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida.
Jason Reding Quiñones has stepped down as the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida, bringing an abrupt end to his leadership of one of the country's most prominent federal prosecutor's offices.
Quiñones announced his resignation on Friday, confirming that his departure would take effect immediately. However, he did not provide a specific reason for leaving the Miami-based office, which has faced growing internal challenges and political controversy during his tenure.
His exit comes as the office faces scrutiny over its involvement in an investigation concerning alleged efforts by former federal officials to undermine President Donald Trump. He was leading the so-called “grand conspiracy” investigation into intelligence officials from the Obama and Biden administrations.
The controversy surrounding the investigation, along with concerns about the office's working environment, has placed Quiñones' leadership under increased scrutiny.
Resignation follows period of internal turmoil
Quiñones' departure comes against the backdrop of reported tensions within the Southern District of Florida's U.S. Attorney's Office. Prosecutors have raised concerns about staff departures, falling morale and limited resources.
Despite announcing his departure without offering an explanation, Quiñones reflected positively on his years of public service in a statement.
"From serving our Nation in uniform to serving at the Department of Justice and on the bench, public service has been the honor of my lifetime," he wrote.
“I am grateful to President Trump for his trust and to the extraordinary men and women of the great Southern District of Florida for their dedication, friendship, and unwavering commitment to justice and the rule of law,” Quiñones said.
“It has been the privilege of a lifetime to serve alongside them and our law enforcement officers who work tirelessly to keep our communities safe.”
He also described leading the federal prosecutor's office in his home district as a particularly significant experience, saying, “But leading the U.S. Attorney’s Office in my home district has been especially meaningful.”

Departure comes after another senior DOJ exit
Quiñones' resignation was announced just one day after the Justice Department confirmed that Harmeet Dhillon, who headed its Civil Rights Division as assistant attorney general, was also leaving her position.
The closely timed departures come amid developments within the Justice Department and renewed attention on the leadership and direction of key federal prosecutorial offices.
While Quiñones has not publicly disclosed the circumstances behind his decision, his sudden exit adds another significant leadership change to the department's recent developments.
His departure also leaves questions about the future leadership of the Southern District of Florida and how the office will address concerns surrounding staffing, morale and its ongoing investigations.
All we know about Trump's election conspiracy probe
Quiñones' resignation marks another setback for the federal investigation being conducted in Fort Pierce, Florida. The probe is examining allegations that former intelligence officials serving under two Democratic administrations coordinated efforts to prevent Donald Trump from remaining in or returning to the White House through a series of criminal and intelligence investigations.
A separate part of the inquiry is examining whether former CIA Director John Brennan provided false testimony to Congress regarding the agency's involvement in preparing an intelligence assessment that concluded Russia had attempted to interfere in the 2016 U.S. presidential election.
The investigation has also faced internal challenges. Earlier this year, the senior career prosecutor in Quiñones' office who was leading the inquiry was removed from her role after reportedly raising questions about the strength of the available evidence, according to CBS News.
Although the investigation has involved significant grand jury proceedings, it has not yet resulted in criminal charges proving the existence of the alleged broader conspiracy.

sources.news_title: Trump's DOJ Hit by Major Exodus After Midterm Disaster — Three Top Officials Resign, Including Prosecutor Behind His Revenge Campaign
sources.text:
The fallout from Republicans’ crushing midterm defeat is already reaching the Justice Department. Three high-profile officials have now resigned, including the federal prosecutor who oversaw one of Donald Trump’s most politically charged efforts to investigate his perceived enemies.
Jason Reding Quiñones, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida, resigned Friday after a troubled tenure overseeing what Trump allies called a “grand conspiracy” investigation targeting officials involved in earlier investigations of the president.
He joins John Eisenberg, who led the Justice Department’s National Security Division and also resigned Friday, and Harmeet Dhillon, the head of the Civil Rights Division, who announced her departure Thursday, The New York Times reports.
The departures came immediately after Democrats swept the midterms and took control of Congress, setting the stage for aggressive oversight and investigations into the Trump administration.
The Prosecutor Behind Trump’s ‘Grand Conspiracy’ Investigation Is Out
Quiñones was at the center of an effort to build a sweeping case against former government officials who investigated Trump and his 2016 presidential campaign.
The so-called “grand conspiracy” inquiry was supposed to examine alleged wrongdoing by officials involved in the Russia investigation and other probes of Trump between 2016 and 2024.
But despite promises that the investigation could produce a major case within months, it failed to deliver the criminal charges Trump allies had been anticipating.
According to people familiar with the situation, Justice Department leadership had become increasingly frustrated with Quiñones, not only over the lack of progress on the politically sensitive investigation but also over his management of one of the department’s most important U.S. attorney’s offices.
The Southern District of Florida handles major drug-trafficking, gang, and national security investigations. Yet Quiñones was reportedly viewed by some colleagues as ineffective and had increasingly been sidelined from sensitive matters, with senior Justice Department deputy Aakash Singh taking over much of that work.
Attorney General Todd Blanche announced Quiñones’s departure on social media Friday. His statement praised the prosecutor’s work on violent crime, drug trafficking, sex trafficking, transnational crime, and the indictment of former Cuban President Raúl Castro.
Notably absent was any mention of the grand conspiracy investigation.
The other departures add to the growing shake-up inside a Justice Department that has spent Trump’s second term pursuing an aggressive agenda shaped by the president’s priorities.
Eisenberg, who headed the National Security Division, resigned Friday. His departure leaves another major leadership vacancy at a department already facing questions about its direction and its handling of politically sensitive investigations.
Dhillon’s exit came a day earlier.
As head of the Civil Rights Division, she oversaw a sweeping transformation of the department’s traditional civil rights priorities, including a major shift toward the administration’s agenda on diversity programs, transgender policies, religious issues, and election-related investigations.
Her tenure also saw a massive departure of career attorneys from the division.
Dhillon has said she planned to return to private practice and had informed the White House of her intention to leave before the midterms. She said she agreed to remain until after Election Day.
Democrats Are About to Have a Much Bigger Say
The departures come as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress, giving them subpoena power, investigative authority, and a much stronger position to scrutinize the Trump administration.
That could make the next two years particularly uncomfortable for officials who played central roles in the administration’s most controversial legal and political initiatives.
Even after leaving government, former officials could still face congressional questions about their decisions and the operations they oversaw.
The resignations could also create a confirmation headache for the White House. With Democrats controlling the Senate, installing permanent replacements for senior positions could become considerably more difficult. Trump can still rely on acting officials in many roles, but that is not the same as having a fully staffed leadership team.
And for the prosecutor who was supposed to help deliver Trump’s long-promised reckoning with his political enemies, the departure comes without the blockbuster conspiracy case his investigation was expected to produce.

sources.news_title: Two More Senior Officials Leave the DOJ
sources.text:
Two top Justice Department officials resigned Friday, creating new vacancies as the White House stares down incoming Democratic control of the Senate confirmation process.
Jason Reding Quiñones, the U.S. attorney in South Florida overseeing the Justice Department’s “grand conspiracy” investigation of President Donald Trump’s political enemies, announced his resignation on social media, saying it was effective immediately.
Soon after, Attorney General Todd Blanche said he had accepted the resignation of John Eisenberg, the assistant attorney general in charge of the DOJ’s National Security Division.
Their departures came a day after Harmeet Dhillon, the Civil Rights Division chief, became the first senior official to resign from the Trump administration after Republicans’ sweeping losses in the midterms.
Trending
The Justice Department has been at the forefront of Trump’s retribution campaign since he returned to the White House last year, and congressional Democrats have made clear they plan to use their new oversight powers to scrutinize a range of actions by Trump’s appointees.
All three new DOJ vacancies are for Senate-confirmed roles. No senior officials from other agencies have yet publicly announced plans to step down in the wake of Democratic victories Tuesday.
Reding Quiñones’ resignation is the latest in a series of departures in the DOJ’s sputtering “Russiagate” probe into claims that Obama-era national security officials conspired to undermine Trump’s rights in the runup to the 2016 election.
Reding Quiñones was the first U.S. attorney confirmed after Trump returned to the White House, and he was tasked with pursuing possible charges against former CIA Director John Brennan and others involved in the investigation of the Trump campaign’s ties to the Russian government in 2016.
He also led a “grand conspiracy” inquiry into former special prosecutor Jack Smith’s decision to charge Trump with mishandling classified documents after his first presidency. Reding Quiñones argued in court papers this year that the indictment was “unlawful” and that a report on Smith’s findings should remain sealed.
To date, nobody has been charged in that investigation. But multiple prominent DOJ officials who worked on it have left recently, including Joseph diGenova, who served as counselor to the attorney general, and Kurt Olsen, who had previously helped Trump’s 2020 election denial efforts.
“Jason Reding Quñiones will forever be known as this president’s Don Quixote for tilting at the windmill of the so-called grand conspiracy,” said Stacey Young, head of the DOJ alumni group Justice Connection and a former attorney with the department. “His departure follows the well-tread path of others who signed up for this impossible dream.”
Reding Quiñones also oversaw several high-profile criminal cases brought under Trump, including the indictment of Raul Castro, the former Cuban president, in connection with the 1996 shooting down of two U.S. civilian rescue planes.
Eisenberg was in charge of the DOJ’s sprawling counterterrorism, intelligence and cybersecurity portfolio. Scores of experienced prosecutors were forced out or left the National Security Division in the period surrounding Eisenberg’s confirmation in June of last year. U.S. attorney overseeing Trump conspiracy probe resigns
WASHINGTON >> The U.S. attorney who had overseen a centerpiece of President Donald Trump’s retribution campaign, the so-called grand conspiracy inquiry of Obama-era officials, has resigned amid growing dissatisfaction with his performance, people familiar with the situation said.
Attorney General Todd Blanche announced the departure of the prosecutor, Jason Reding Quiñones, on social media. He is among the first of what is expected to be a succession of departures at the Justice Department after the midterm elections Tuesday.
Blanche, in making the announcement, did not mention Reding Quiñones’ work on the grand conspiracy case, but instead cited his efforts on violent crime, drugs and the indictment of former Cuban leader Raúl Castro.
Reding Quiñones, a close ally of influential right-wing lawyer Mike Davis, had long been viewed as ineffective and had largely been marginalized. Many of the office’s most sensitive investigations were already being overseen by a top Blanche deputy, Aakash Singh, according to three people with knowledge of the situation who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal matters.
Officials were frustrated not only with Reding Quiñones’ inability to demonstrate progress on the grand conspiracy cases but with his troubled stewardship of a marquee U.S. attorney’s office responsible for major drug and gang investigations.
Reding Quiñones did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but he thanked Trump on social media. “I am grateful to President Trump for his trust and to the extraordinary men and women of the great Southern District of Florida for their dedication, friendship, and unwavering commitment to justice and the rule of law,” he wrote.
Don't miss out on what's happening!
Stay in touch with breaking news, as it happens, conveniently in your email inbox. It's FREE!
Reding Quiñones presided over an office in deep crisis. The Southern District had more than 200 lawyers when he arrived, but by the fall, it fell to slightly more than half that number, after a spate of firings and resignations.
So many career prosecutors have fled that Reding Quiñones, an Army reservist, was forced to bring in military lawyers to backfill the ranks.
Reding Quiñones is at least the third U.S. attorney in the Trump administration to step down after being assigned to investigate all or part of the “grand conspiracy.” The catchall term has been used by Trump loyalists to describe the effort to file criminal charges against former Obama administration officials, intelligence veterans and Democratic operatives for purportedly misusing their positions to harm Trump.
Two U.S. attorneys in Virginia were forced out of their jobs last year, having displeased senior Trump administration officials by concluding that criminal charges were not warranted against figures such as former FBI director James Comey.
In Reding Quiñones, the Justice Department found a prosecutor willing to pursue the investigation further, with the help of a judge who had proved herself amenable to Trump’s legal arguments: Judge Aileen Cannon in Fort Pierce, Florida.
But the investigation has not fared much better. A career Justice Department official in Miami who oversaw the case concluded that there was not sufficient evidence to support criminal charges against John Brennan, the former CIA director, and was subsequently removed from the case.
The administration brought in a veteran former prosecutor, Joseph DiGenova, who proceeded to slowly retrace the previous investigations. Senior administration officials grew frustrated with what they viewed as the snail’s pace of DiGenova’s work, and he left under pressure in September.
Another Trump loyalist assigned to the case left weeks later, and senior officials have privately expressed frustration with Reding Quiñones’ handling of the case.
In October, the Justice Department filed new charges in Washington — without a grand jury indictment or a judge’s signature — against Comey, accusing him of directing a leak of classified information to a New York Times reporter in 2016. Comey has denied the accusation and is seeking to have the case dismissed.

Top Trump DOJ Prosecutor Jason Reding Quiñones Resigns Amid Investigation Into Russiagate Controversy
Jason Reding Quiñones, the federal prosecutor overseeing a major Justice Department investigation into allegations of misconduct surrounding the Russia investigation targeting President Trump, has officially resigned. His departure marks another significant leadership change within the Trump administration’s Justice Department, coming just days after Republicans suffered major losses in the 2026 midterm elections.
Attorney General Todd Blanche announced the resignation Friday, thanking Quiñones for his service as U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida. Blanche praised his leadership in combating violent crime, drug trafficking, sex trafficking, and international criminal organizations, highlighting his involvement in a high-profile case against former Cuban leader Raúl Castro.
Quiñones confirmed that his resignation was effective immediately, expressing gratitude to President Trump for the opportunity to serve. He described his time leading the federal prosecutor’s office in his home district as a tremendous honor and thanked the attorneys, investigators, and law enforcement officers who worked alongside him. He did not publicly identify a specific reason for stepping down.
The resignation carries particular significance because Quiñones had been entrusted with overseeing one of the Justice Department’s most politically sensitive investigations. The inquiry examines whether officials from previous Democratic administrations engaged in coordinated misconduct involving investigations of President Trump, including the FBI’s examination of alleged connections between his 2016 presidential campaign and Russia.
The investigation, frequently described as the grand conspiracy probe, was launched in August 2025 to examine allegations that senior government officials improperly used federal intelligence and law enforcement institutions against Trump. Investigators have scrutinized decisions made during the Obama and Biden administrations, including the origins of the Russia investigation and subsequent federal investigations involving the president.
Among the prominent figures examined are former CIA Director John Brennan, former Director of National Intelligence James Clapper, and former FBI Director James Comey. Federal investigators have issued subpoenas seeking testimony and records concerning intelligence assessments, investigative decisions, and the conduct of officials involved in examining Russian interference in the 2016 election.
A major component of the inquiry concerns the intelligence community’s assessment of Russian election interference and whether officials misrepresented information during congressional testimony. Brennan has faced particular scrutiny over statements concerning the CIA’s role in preparing the assessment. His attorneys have rejected allegations of wrongdoing, while investigators have continued examining whether any federal laws were violated.
The investigation has encountered substantial internal disagreements over its scope, management, and the evidence necessary to pursue criminal charges. Several prosecutors assigned to the inquiry have departed, raising questions about the pace of the investigation and the Justice Department’s ability to move forward with potential indictments.
Former federal prosecutor Joe diGenova, who had been selected to help lead the investigation, resigned in September following disagreements over the handling of the case. Another prominent attorney associated with the inquiry, Kurt Olsen, subsequently departed. Their exits contributed to uncertainty surrounding an investigation that has attracted considerable attention from President Trump’s political allies.
Despite months of investigative activity, the broader conspiracy inquiry has not produced the sweeping criminal indictments that some Trump allies had anticipated. The absence of charges has intensified questions about whether prosecutors have obtained sufficient evidence to establish criminal wrongdoing by former intelligence and law enforcement officials.
Quiñones’ resignation also follows the departure of Harmeet Dhillon, who stepped down Thursday as head of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division. The two resignations represent significant changes in the department’s senior leadership immediately following the midterm elections, although neither departure has been publicly established as a direct consequence of the Republican defeat.

His office pursued cases involving organized crime, immigration offenses, financial misconduct, narcotics trafficking, and national security threats. The case drew particular attention in South Florida, where Cuban American communities have long demanded accountability for the deaths of four men aboard the aircraft.
Quiñones, a military veteran and former Florida judge, was among President Trump’s earliest confirmed U.S. attorney appointments during his second administration. His selection reflected the president’s effort to install prosecutors committed to strengthening federal law enforcement and reviewing controversies involving previous administrations.
Following his resignation, First Assistant U.S. Attorney Yara Klukas is expected to assume leadership of the Southern District of Florida on an acting basis. According to reporting citing a person familiar with the matter, the Justice Department intends to continue the grand conspiracy investigation under her supervision, although its future direction remains uncertain.

President Trump has repeatedly questioned the conduct of officials involved in the original Russia investigation, and the Justice Department’s examination of those allegations remains an important issue for his administration.
Quiñones leaves office with a record that includes major criminal prosecutions, organizational restructuring, and oversight of an investigation into one of the most contentious political controversies of Trump’s presidency.
